description: Pinpointing the specific acting choices that communicate character and meaning to an audience.
content_html:
From Feeling to Technique

When a performer moves an audience to tears, the temptation is to write “they were convincingly upset.” That sentence earns no marks. The exam rewards you for explaining how the performer created that effect: the precise vocal and physical skills they deployed and the meaning those skills communicated at that specific moment.

Vocal skills and physical skills are the two categories the spec identifies. Top-mark answers always name at least one from each category, anchor them to a specific moment in the production, and explain the effect on the audience.

Key Fact

Vocal skills include: pitch, pace, pause, volume, accent, intonation, phrasing, projection and timing. Physical skills include: posture, gesture, facial expression, movement, stillness, gait, spatial awareness and interaction with other performers.

Vocal Skills: The Language of Voice

Each vocal skill can be used to create a specific effect. Knowing which skill creates which effect is the key to strong analytical writing. Consider these:

  • Pitch: a sudden rise in pitch signals panic or excitement; a drop to the low register can convey threat, grief or resignation. The contrast between the two within a single speech is itself a technique — it shows the character’s instability.
  • Pace: rapid delivery can signal urgency or desperation; a deliberate, unhurried pace can communicate authority, menace or exhaustion. A performer who slows dramatically at the climax of a speech draws the audience in.
  • Pause: a well-placed silence is one of the most powerful tools a performer has. A three-second pause before a character’s answer can communicate internal conflict more precisely than any amount of text. Think of it as a word the playwright left blank for the performer to fill.
  • Volume: a performer who drops from normal conversational volume to near-inaudible draws the audience physically forward in their seats; a sudden shout after sustained quiet is a physical shock. Both are intentional choices.
  • Intonation and phrasing: the rising or falling melody of a sentence, and where the performer chooses to breathe and break their line, controls where the audience focuses its attention.

Physical Skills: The Language of the Body

Tableau and stillness are often more powerful than movement. When a performer freezes in the middle of chaotic action, every audience member looks at them immediately. That is focus achieved through physical discipline, not scenery.

Other physical skills to analyse include:

  • Posture: an upright, expansive posture reads as power or confidence across the room; a collapsed, inward posture reads as vulnerability or defeat. If the posture shifts within a scene, the character’s status has shifted — note exactly when it changes.
  • Gesture: gestures can be open (arms extended, palms up — invitation) or closed (arms crossed, hands pulled in — self-protection). A single raised hand can silence a stage; a pointing finger can be an accusation. Analyse the gesture, not just its name.
  • Facial expression: the micro-expressions that pass across a performer’s face in a close-focus moment are often what an audience remembers most vividly. If the performer’s expression contradicted the character’s words — a smile that didn’t reach the eyes, a flash of doubt suppressed — that subtext is gold for analysis.
  • Movement and gait: how a character crosses the stage communicates as much as what they say. A heavy, deliberate walk implies weight (emotional or literal); a light, darting movement implies anxiety or calculation.

Imagine you saw a fictional touring production of a kitchen-sink drama in 2024. In the climactic argument scene, the lead performer playing the mother confronted the adult son. Here is how you might write about that moment:

Weak version (no marks at this level): “The actress playing the mother was very emotional and you could tell she was upset. She looked like she was going to cry.”

Strong version: “In the moment when the mother finally confronted her son, the performer dropped her vocal pace to almost half its previous rate and allowed a three-beat pause after each sentence, as though each word cost her something. Simultaneously, her physical posture collapsed inward — shoulders drawn forward, spine curved, eyes cast downward rather than meeting his — so that despite her status as parent, she visually occupied less stage space than her adult son. This juxtaposition — a parent whose voice is measured and powerful but whose body has surrendered — communicated the complexity of her grief: she was both holding herself together and falling apart simultaneously. The audience became very still at this moment, which suggested the choice was communicating its intended meaning effectively.”

Notice: one vocal skill (pace and pause), one physical skill (posture and use of stage space), a specific moment, a named effect on the audience, and an evaluative judgement. That is the formula for a top-band paragraph.

Interaction and Ensemble

In your review, do not only write about individual performers in isolation. Ensemble moments — where the company moves, speaks or responds as a single unit — are often the most theatrically powerful. When an ensemble suddenly splits apart, or when all performers simultaneously turn to face the audience, the effect is difficult to achieve and, when it works, is deeply affecting.

Analyse the interaction between two performers as you would a single performer: what did the proxemics between them tell you? Did one performer physically diminish themselves to elevate the other? Did a brief moment of eye contact or its conspicuous absence change the mood of the scene?

A persistent error is to describe the character’s inner state rather than the performer’s external technique. Phrases like “she was angry,” “he seemed afraid” and “you could feel her sadness” describe emotions, not skills. They tell the examiner nothing about how the performer communicated the emotion.

The fix is simple: ask yourself, “what did the performer actually do with their voice or body?” Then describe that. “She was angry” becomes “her volume escalated across the scene until by the final line she was projecting at full strength from upstage right, her jaw tense and her hands forming fists at her sides.” That is performer technique, not emotional description.

Key Fact

Every time you write about a performer, you need both a vocal AND a physical choice. One alone is not enough for an 8-mark or 32-mark answer. Train yourself to pair them: “vocally she… / physically she…”
exam_tip_html:
For questions asking you to interpret or analyse a performer, the most common error is to write about what the character is feeling without translating that into specific vocal and physical choices. “I would act scared” is not a technique; “I would lower my volume to a near-whisper, increase the pace of my delivery and physically back away to upstage right while maintaining eye contact with the antagonist” is.

Always pair vocal and physical: the examiner looks for both. If you only address one category, you cannot reach the top band regardless of how detailed you are. A useful self-check: count your vocal skills and your physical skills in your draft answer. If either column is empty, add to it before you move on.

In the 32-mark live theatre review, anchor every performer observation to a named moment (not “throughout the play”). The more specific the moment, the more analytical your writing can be.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Performer analysis requires both vocal skills (pitch, pace, pause, volume, intonation, phrasing) and physical skills (posture, gesture, facial expression, movement, stillness) — always name one of each and anchor them to a specific moment.
  • Describe what the performer did, not how the character felt: “she lowered her pitch and allowed a three-beat pause” is analytical; “she seemed sad” is not.
  • Ensemble interaction and proxemics between performers are equally valid subjects for analysis — the spatial relationship between two characters at a key moment can communicate meaning as powerfully as any single performer choice.

practice_questions.text: Identify one vocal skill a performer might use to communicate a character's authority.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: a slow, measured pace / a low pitch / a loud, projected volume / a deliberate pause before speaking / a clipped, precise intonation. Accept any precise vocal skill linked plausibly to authority.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'tableau'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it is a still, frozen stage picture; 1 mark for explaining that it uses the positions and relationships of performers' bodies to communicate meaning without movement or speech.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer's use of stillness at a key moment in a live production can have a powerful effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what stillness is (a deliberate absence of movement at a chosen moment); 1 mark for explaining how it draws focus (the eye is drawn to the still performer amid movement, or to the performer whose stillness signals internal change); 1 mark for a specific audience effect (e.g. the audience becomes quiet, leans in, anticipates what comes next); 1 mark for a developed link to meaning or character (e.g. stillness can communicate suppressed emotion, moral weight or a moment of decision more powerfully than action).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the interaction between two performers in the live production you have seen communicated the relationship between their characters at a specific moment.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for naming a specific moment or scene; 1 mark for identifying a specific interaction (e.g. one performer's gaze held, broken or avoided; the proxemic distance decreasing or increasing; a gesture directed at rather than away from the other); 1 mark for analytical development of what the interaction communicated about the characters' relationship (power, intimacy, conflict, dependency); 1 mark for a statement about audience effect or evaluative comment on how effectively the relationship was communicated.

practice_questions.text: Imagine you saw a fictional community theatre production of a tragedy in 2025. In the final scene, the lead performer playing the protagonist discovers they have caused the death of someone they loved. As a performer in that role, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate the character's shock and guilt to the audience. Refer to specific vocal and physical skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Names at least one precise vocal choice (e.g. voice drops to near-silence; all pace is stripped away so delivery becomes word by single word; a sharp intake of breath before speech begins) AND at least one precise physical choice (e.g. the body sinks from standing to crouching over the figure on the floor; hands reach out but stop short of touching; the face tilts up toward the audience then immediately turns away), both anchored clearly to this discovery moment; the effect on the audience is named and substantiated (e.g. the silence in the auditorium confirmed the audience was holding this moment with the performer); language is technically fluent throughout.
Secure (5-6): Names a vocal and a physical choice, generally anchored to the moment; audience effect explained for at least one choice; mostly specific but may contain one general descriptor.
Developing (3-4): Relevant choices present but described in general or emotional terms; little technical vocabulary; limited link to audience effect.
Emerging (1-2): Basic emotional description with no technical vocabulary and no specific moment or audience effect identified.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. Focus specifically on the vocal and physical choices made by one performer in a key moment. Explain how those choices communicated meaning and evaluate how successfully they worked for the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Sustained analytical writing focused on a clearly named moment; at least two vocal choices and at least two physical choices are named with technical precision (not just 'louder' but 'projected from the diaphragm with the volume rising across the final three lines'); each choice is linked to a specific, named audience effect; an evaluative judgement is reached that is substantiated by the evidence given; terminology used accurately and fluently throughout.
Secure (17-24): At least one vocal and one physical choice named and explained with effect; some technical vocabulary; evaluative judgement present though may not be fully substantiated; generally anchored to a specific moment.
Developing (9-16): Choices identified but described in general emotional terms; some relevant vocabulary; some attempt at audience effect; limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-8): Largely descriptive or plot-based; minimal technical vocabulary; no evaluative judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a physical skill, not a vocal skill?
When analysing a performer for an extended-response question, which two categories of skill must always both be included?
A tableau is a _____, motionless stage picture using performers to communicate meaning through body position.
In analysis, instead of writing 'she was angry', you should write about the specific _____ and _____ choices the performer made.
Match each vocal skill to its potential effect on the audience:
left: A sudden drop in volume to near-whisper
right: Communicates internal conflict or weight of decision
Draws the audience in and creates tension or intimacy
Communicates urgency, desperation or building panic

flashcard_questions.a: Techniques a performer uses with their voice: pitch, pace, pause, volume, intonation, phrasing, accent.
Techniques a performer uses with their body: posture, gesture, facial expression, movement, stillness, gait.
A still, frozen stage picture communicating meaning through performers' body positions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is stage space (in relation to a performer)?
flashcard_questions.a: The area a performer occupies; larger space suggests higher status or confidence.
The physical and emotional distance between two performers, signalling their relationship.
Performers working as a unified group, sharing focus rather than one performer dominating.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is 'she was angry' not a valid analysis of a performer?
flashcard_questions.a: It describes emotion, not technique. Analysis must name the specific vocal or physical skill used.

flashcard_questions.q: What effect can a deliberate pause create for the audience?
flashcard_questions.a: Tension, anticipation, or the sense of a character weighing a decision.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one physical skill that can communicate a character's high status.
flashcard_questions.a: Upright, expansive posture; or deliberately slow, controlled movement.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must you name at least one vocal AND one physical skill in a performer analysis answer?
flashcard_questions.a: The mark scheme requires both categories; one alone cannot reach the top band.
The rising or falling melody of a performer's speech, controlling where the audience places attention.

flashcard_questions.q: How can a performer use eye contact or its absence to communicate character relationship?
flashcard_questions.a: Sustained eye contact implies intimacy or challenge; averted gaze implies guilt, fear or submission.

glossary_terms.definition: The measurable technical skills a performer uses with their voice to communicate character, emotion and meaning, including pitch, pace, pause, volume, intonation, phrasing and accent.
The measurable technical skills a performer uses with their body to communicate character, status and emotion, including posture, gesture, facial expression, movement, stillness and eye contact.
A held, motionless stage picture using one or more performers, communicating status, relationship or emotion through body position alone.
The area a performer occupies on stage; larger stage space implies higher status or confidence, while smaller stage space implies vulnerability or submission.
The physical and emotional distance between two performers on stage at a given moment, used to signal their relationship.
A group of performers working together as a unified company, sharing focus and movement rather than one performer dominating.
The manner in which a performer walks across the stage, used to communicate character status, mood or physical condition.
The unstated meaning beneath a character's words, communicated by the performer through vocal and physical choices rather than the script itself.
